en: Devātiśayastotra:
Homage to the Buddha.
The Blessed One, the Sugata, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha are not perceived through direct perception; yet,
[one may know them] by means of their forms, deeds, excellences, and powers.
Having heard this, investigate whether he possesses virtue or not. ||1||
Viṣṇu has a hand terrible with a raised mace-weapon;
Śambhu wears a garland of skulls topped with the head of a man;
but the Buddha is one whose conduct is characterized by the excellence of absolute tranquility.
Whom shall I worship—the peaceful one or the one whose form is unpeaceful? ||2||
Viṣṇu became the destroyer of the lineage beginning with Duryodhana; indeed, Hara was the burner of Tripura;
and Guha likewise struck down Krauñca with his firm spear.
But the Buddhas alone are those who desire the welfare of the world. ||3||
"This one is to be oppressed by me, but this very one must be protected;
this one is to be slain"— this is the policy of the best of gods,
whose singular intellect is intent on the welfare of the happiness of ultimate liberation and worldly prosperity.
For the Buddha, there are no enemies, nor is he to be deceived. ||4||
The words of Viṣṇu give rise to defects such as passion;
likewise, those of Śambhu produce the behavior of a madman;
but those of the Tathāgata pacify all defects without exception.
And who here deserves to be honored? Reflect upon this.
He who is intent on slaying his enemies, having cast aside compassion; and he who is engaged in protecting the world out of mercy;
he who is full of passion, and he who is liberated from passion.
Having reflected upon these two, tell me, who indeed here is worthy of worship? (6)
Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt; Bala, the wielder of the plow; Viṣṇu, whose weapon is the discus;
Skanda, the wielder of the spear; and the one whose abode is the cremation ground.
Rudra, armed with the trident;
these [demons], devoid of compassion, afflicted by suffering and fear,
and possessing various weapons, [assailed] the children.
What wise person would pay homage to those who are constantly raising weapons with the intent to kill living beings? (7)
He who does not bear a trident, nor a fair-faced young woman upon his lap, nor a discus or a spear;
Neither the fierce thunderbolt nor the plow [is as formidable] as one whose mind is intent on accomplishing the welfare of others and who is liberated from the afflictions.
I have come for refuge to that sage, the protector of the worlds. ||8||
Rudra, driven by the force of passion, carries a woman; he is violent, devoid of shame,
more cruel than Viṣṇu, and his conduct is that of an ungrateful man.
Skanda himself is the destroyer of ignorance;
Pārvatī, who brings an end to Mahiṣa, is fierce in her aspirations and consumes human fat and flesh.
And since the Guide desires only to drink, what fault could there be, even if it were very slight, in the One Possessing Ten Powers? (9)
That Blessed One is neither our kinsman nor are others our enemies;
not even one among them has been directly seen before. Yet, having heard their very beautiful words, each with its distinct particularity—
We have taken refuge in the Buddha out of a longing for his preeminent qualities. ||10||
The Sugata is not our father, nor are the heretics our enemies; neither was wealth given to us by that Tathāgata, nor was it taken away.
Some [teachings] were taught by Kaṇāda and others;
however, that Blessed One, the Buddha, is solely devoted to the welfare of the world, and from him [comes] the stainless [teaching].
And since that speech removes all impurities,
we are therefore devoted to it.
He who is always desirous of the welfare [of others] and constantly a benefactor to the world,
by whom health has been established;
To him, for whom the entire world— afflicted by manifold diseases—
appears clearly as if it were the palm of his hand, all that is to be known is manifest.
He [saw] that incomparable seer with a mind full of devotion. || 12 ||
Whether with incomplete devotion, or through medical treatment,
or by following the lead of others, or even with doubt— those who pay homage to you, O Moon among the Lords of Sages, [attain liberation].
They too attain the perfection of immortality. ||13||
This ancient Vedic revelation is that the Buddha, honored by the world, was indeed Hari himself;
having perceived birth, old age, destruction, and frailty, [he appeared].
The protector of men, Gautama, born from the lord of the Śākya clan, possessing wondrous intelligence, has arisen for the world, intent upon compassion.
Who that is unwise or deluded would not recognize him as the Teacher who is truly beneficial? When [one is overcome] by passion and hatred... 14... [then...]
The abduction of the daughters of the Asuras and Suras was carried out by that one of unattached mind, who, through his mastery of illusion, lifted up the earth.
At that time, even Hari— who is worthy of worship and salutation and is himself liberated from ignorance—
is not honored by people who are full of delusion. ||15||
Having relinquished to Hari the earth, which was weary from the burden of its shell-like continents girdled by the four oceans, Bali—
King Aśoka fell into a miserable state after offering a mere handful of dust as a funeral ball to his son Maṇi.
He reached the earth, which had the surface of the full moon as its silken garment. ||16||
I have no partiality for the Buddha, nor do I harbor hatred toward Kapila and others;
he alone is to be accepted as the one whose purpose must be accomplished. 17.
Necessarily, among all these Victors, one or another whose teaching is exclusively vast for the welfare of the world must surely be seen with the subtle eye of intelligence.
What is the use of meeting with all those who are experts in what is meaningless? ||18||
He in whom all defects are absent and all virtues are present—
be he Brahmā or Viṣṇu.
Or that Maheśvara is my teacher. ||19||
He in whom no faults are found,
in whom immeasurable virtues exist,
who is omniscient and compassionate.
I have gone to him for refuge. ||20||
Thus, having praised the Buddha— who is like an ocean to the rivers of thousands of praises— with eyes as broad as the petals of a blossomed lotus,
whatever merit there may be in me arising from these words, [may it be for the benefit of all beings].
May all beings born thereby indeed become happy.
The *Devātiśayastotra* is completed.
This is the work of the teacher, Bhaṭṭa Varāhasvāmin.
